title: The Maidams of Charaideo Remember the Dead

title_i18n.en: The Maidams of Charaideo Remember the Dead

subtitle: Beneath the Green Domes of Charaideo
figure: The Chang-Rung Phukan and Rudra Singha
era: Royal burials from the 13th to 18th centuries; UNESCO inscription 2023
moral: A society honors the past best when it also learns to leave cruelty behind.

sources.citation: ASI Guwahati Circle, Excavation at Maidam No. 2, Charaideo (2002)
sources.note: Recent excavation evidence for brick vaults, skeletal remains, ivory objects and looting.

sources.citation: UNESCO World Heritage Committee, Charaideo Maidams, Decision 45COM 8B.28 (2023)
sources.note: Most recent heritage documentation and inscription of the site.

sources.citation: Chang-Rung Phukanor Buranji, Assam architectural chronicle tradition
sources.note: Primary textual tradition for tomb construction procedures and materials.

panels.shot: wide aerial sunset shot over rolling green mounds and broken brick walls on a misty Assam hilltop

dialogue.text: On the hill of Charaideo, where Tai chiefs slept under earth and brick, an architect and a king quietly rewrote how the Ahoms would remember the dead.

panels.shot: slow push-in on one massive maidam mound rising from early-morning fog, with forest beyond

dialogue.text: Here, from the thirteenth to the eighteenth century, the Ahom rulers raised earthen domes over brick vaults, turning Charaideo into a city of the dead that watched over a living kingdom.

panels.shot: cutaway wide shot imagining an early 13th-century scene, slightly elevated angle over a small Tai-Ahom settlement

dialogue.text: In the early days, when the Tai-Ahom chiefs first chose Charaideo as their capital, their burials were humbler, closer to their south-east Asian homelands, yet already set apart on the sacred hill.

panels.shot: medium shot of Chang-Rung Phukan seated indoors at a low table, manuscripts and tools spread around, lit by lamplight

dialogue.text: Generations later, the Chang-Rung Phukan, the royal architect, gathered what practice and memory knew into a buranji, setting down how a maidam must rise, brick by brick, ritual by ritual.

panels.shot: cutaway cross-section wide shot, half above ground and half below, showing the internal structure of a maidam

dialogue.text: The buranji describes a buried brick chamber, sometimes with multiple rooms and pillars, sealed and covered by earth, then ringed by an octagonal wall: a palace for the dead beneath a green dome.

panels.shot: low-angle wide shot of labourers constructing an octagonal wall in brick, forest and sky beyond

dialogue.text: Brickmakers, masons and earth-workers turned the architect’s lines into walls and mounds, so that each Ahom king and noble would lie within a carefully measured geometry of power and memory.

panels.shot: dim interior medium shot inside a newly completed vault, lit by oil lamps, with attendants placing objects

dialogue.text: The Ahom chronicles speak of treasured objects sent below; centuries later, excavations at a maidam would uncover ivory panels and wooden pieces, echoes of those recorded funeral furnishings.

panels.shot: wide ritual courtyard shot, with priests and officials arrayed around the maidam, river valley visible in distance

dialogue.text: Around the maidams, officers held titles tied to the dead, and rites linked the buried rulers with the living realm, for the Ahoms believed that kings did not simply vanish beneath the hill.

panels.shot: tight medium shot of a small group of bound attendants near a burial site, faces fearful, guards impassive

dialogue.text: Yet the same texts also whisper of a darker duty: in earlier times, some attendants were sent alive into the vault, buried with their lord, the ultimate sign of loyalty and a terrible cost.

panels.shot: dramatic throne-room medium shot of Rudra Singha, slightly low angle, courtiers around, heavy beams overhead

dialogue.text: When Rudra Singha ruled in the early eighteenth century, the buranjis credit him with a quiet revolution: he ordered that no more living attendants be buried with their masters at Charaideo.

panels.shot: medium two-shot of Rudra Singha speaking to Chang-Rung Phukan in a shaded courtyard overlooking distant maidams

dialogue.speaker: the_chang_rung_phukan_and_rudra_singha
dialogue.text: Let the bricks stand, Phukan, but let the living walk out into the sun.

panels.shot: symbolic medium shot of labourers sealing a vault entrance with bricks while freed attendants walk away toward the light

dialogue.text: In the architect’s practice, little changed in brick or earth; but in the lives spared at the door of the vault, the kingdom altered its pact with death while keeping faith with remembrance.

panels.shot: wide shot of a maidam centuries later, partially damaged, with a gaping hole in the mound and scattered bricks

dialogue.text: Time and greed carved their own passages; when archaeologists entered one maidam in our age, they met not untouched stillness but disturbed earth and a vault already wounded by looters.

panels.shot: careful interior medium shot of modern archaeologists inside the vault, kneeling by skeletal remains and objects, soft lantern light

dialogue.text: Even so, the excavation at one maidam revealed five skeletons, ivory and wooden pieces, traces that broadly matched the buranji’s words, though many questions about each tomb still remain.

panels.shot: wide shot of a present-day Me-Dam-Me-Phi ceremony at the foot of the hill, families gathered, offerings laid out

dialogue.text: Each year, in Me-Dam-Me-Phi rites, the living still call upon ancestors, the Ahom tradition of honouring the dead carried forward without burial chambers, turning hill and home into shared sacred space.

panels.shot: contemporary aerial wide shot of Charaideo maidams, with visitors walking on paths and conservation structures visible

dialogue.text: In 2023, the world formally recognised Charaideo’s maidams, yet most lie unexcavated beneath their grass, their stories known only in part, their silence protected as much as it is studied.

panels.shot: low-angle medium shot of Chang-Rung Phukan and Rudra Singha imagined standing together on a modern path between maidams, blending past and present

dialogue.text: Between the architect’s measured bricks and the king’s choice to spare lives, Charaideo teaches that a people can build mighty tombs, yet honour their dead best by loosening death’s hold on the living.
